4
A transmitter emits a pulse of electromagnetic waves towards a reflector. The pulse is reflected
and returns to the transmitter.
A detector is located at the transmitter. The emitted pulse and the reflected pulse are displayed
on a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) as shown.
1 cm
1 cm
The pulse takes 6.3 µs to travel from the transmitter to the reflector.
What is the time-base setting of the CRO?
A
2.1 µs cm–1
B
3.2 µs cm–1
C
4.2 µs cm–1
D
6.3 µs cm–1

hints: Measure the horizontal distance between the same point on the two pulses on the CRO screen - count how many 1 cm divisions separate the emitted pulse peak from the reflected pulse peak.
The $6.3\,\mu\text{s}$ given is only transmitter to reflector, while the CRO time between the two peaks is transmitter to reflector and back to the detector.
Divide the total go-and-return time by the measured cm separation to get time per cm in $\mu\text{s cm}^{-1}$.
walkthrough: Measure the peak-to-peak horizontal separation on the trace. The emitted peak and reflected peak are 3 squares apart, and each square is 1 cm, so separation $= 3.0\,\text{cm}$.
State the physics: the time between the two peaks is the round-trip time. Given one-way time $= 6.3\,\mu\text{s}$, total time $= 2 \times 6.3\,\mu\text{s} = 12.6\,\mu\text{s}$.
Recall time-base $= $ time per unit length $= $ total time / horizontal distance.

A.explanation: Gives about half the correct value, from dividing the $12.6\,\mu\text{s}$ round-trip time by 6 cm instead of the measured 3 cm separation.

B.explanation: Does not follow from $12.6\,\mu\text{s}$ divided by the 3 cm pulse separation on the CRO screen.

C.explanation: The $12.6\,\mu\text{s}$ round-trip time spread over 3 cm gives $12.6/3 = 4.2\,\mu\text{s cm}^{-1}$.

D.explanation: Uses only the one-way $6.3\,\mu\text{s}$ time, forgetting the CRO shows the time for the pulse to go to the reflector and return.
